title: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters
author: Laura Clayton McDonnell

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: McDonnell aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on human verification, domain expertise and employer-supported AI training. However, she does not address the principal claim that automating junior work threatens apprenticeship and expertise reproduction, nor does she propose the cluster’s specific reconstruction through simulation, mentorship and independent practice.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s shift from product announcements to demonstrated workflow fit and control, then materially develops it for agentic AI: it supplies a functional definition, reports that few products meet it, and proposes procurement checks for plan visibility and lawyer intervention before execution.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: McDonnell accepts that legal technology should enable business-facing strategic work rather than stop at document processing. She extends the proposition with examples of routine contract-review automation creating strategic capacity and trade-management data supporting rapid, potentially business-changing advice, while offering only vendor-reported evidence rather than independently validated outcomes.

analyze insights extracted so you can then offer up that kind of advice that is pretty, it’s changing, it’s almost sort of business changing type of advice, especially nowadays, to be able to do it at your fingertips as quickly as the regulatory landscape is changing.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source accepts the need for disciplined vendor selection and materially develops it for agentic products: it defines substantive agent capabilities, warns buyers not to rely on marketing labels, and proposes inspecting whether users can review and redirect an agent’s plan before execution. Its evidence is a panel assessment and practical procurement guidance, not quantitative product testing.
qs: think in light of all the activity in this space, it’s really important for firms to understand what is meant by the term so they can see through marketing language and determine when something really is agentic and when it’s not.

For example, if an agent is operating in a legal workflow, you may want to know whether visibility has been built in so that you can see the plan the agent creates for achieving its overall goal before it gets going on that plan and whether the lawyer or user is able to course correct the plan before it is executed.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: McDonnell accepts the cluster’s core human-led, selective-deployment model and materially develops it through corporate examples of routine-work reduction, strategic capacity creation, tactical sourcing, stakeholder-led transformation, workforce training and reliability testing. She explicitly treats generative and agentic AI as augmentation rather than replacement and retains human professional accountability for outputs.
qs: And I remind some folks too, especially folks who have been in the law field, is that according to the code of professional responsibility, whether you have a paralegal or you have an AI, you’re still responsible.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s cautious augmentation framing: routine automation can free professionals for strategic work, but humans must oversee and verify AI. Her governance, auditing and data-quality recommendations align with the cluster’s emphasis on intervention and control, although she does not directly examine multi-step error propagation or demonstrate agentic reliability.
qs: There’s examples in the past where if you’re not monitoring that, if you’re not auditing it, if you don’t have a review of it, it can go awry, right?

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s core proposition by making domain expertise and human verification conditions for AI value, even as agentic systems approach aspects of human judgment. Her cross-disciplinary scenario adds illustrative scope, but remains hypothetical rather than a concrete workflow or measured finding.
qs: Once again, going back to our earlier conversation about the human still needs to be involved, oversight needs to happen.
And we know that, you know, powered by domain expertise and humans checking, it could be of value.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s proposition that continuous learning can draw on professional networks and situated market knowledge rather than constant release chasing. Her reliance on internal specialists and customers illustrates contextual intelligence, but remains anecdotal and does not establish adoption or effectiveness.
qs: And they’re always good for us to tap into and learn what’s going out there and just keeping up to date.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core emphasis on using technology to free professional capacity for business outcomes and recognises buyer-side budget incentives. However, it offers only qualitative support and does not establish end-to-end delivery redesign, verification practices, pricing changes or solutions to staffing and apprenticeship risks.
qs: Or the workflows that we have, OneSource, Pegaro, Haiku, Legal Tracker, Clear, all of…  which is designed once again to free up time for you to do some things that really do matter in terms of the priorities of that business.

Laura (22:56)  Yeah, I mean, think what, know, especially like the general counsel’s office, the general counsel is really looking to see how can I work with this budget that I’ve been given and still make an impact in an organization.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s core framing of AI as an augmentation and organisational-development challenge rather than straightforward professional replacement. Her emphasis on human oversight, domain expertise, company-supported AI training and continuous learning aligns with the cluster’s proposed response, although she does not directly analyse apprenticeship, leverage or partner succession and offers forecasts rather than measured outcomes.
qs: Once again, going back to our earlier conversation about the human still needs to be involved, oversight needs to happen.
Training that needs to co-sponsor it from your company to help folks learn about AI.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s principal proposition that technology benefits depend on organisational readiness. She pairs company-supported technology use with resilient, high-performing teams that embrace change and continue learning, while offering general guidance rather than measured evidence or a detailed account of human control.
qs: We’re looking for our companies to help us with that because technology is going to be able to be used for us to get ahead.
How do you develop this high performance team that is willing to embrace the changes that occur and be able to continue to deliver and continue to learn?

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s emphasis on institutional readiness and copilot-style use: AI’s value depends on domain expertise, human verification, continuing professional accountability and employer-supported training. Her forecasts about judgment-related capabilities and skilled-worker demand are explicitly prospective rather than measured evidence, consistent with the cluster’s qualification of ambitious predictions.
qs: And we know that, you know, powered by domain expertise and humans checking, it could be of value.
Training that needs to co-sponsor it from your company to help folks learn about AI.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s emphasis on accountable, human-centred deployment rather than treating emerging AI capabilities as established substitutes for legal judgment. She keeps professional responsibility with lawyers and frames predictive and judgment-intensive uses as promising but unproven, with reliability and testing still unresolved.
qs: And I remind some folks too, especially folks who have been in the law field, is that according to the code of professional responsibility, whether you have a paralegal or you have an AI, you’re still responsible.
How do we test to make sure it’s reliable?

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s core view that technology will augment professional work and reshape legal-service allocation rather than autonomously replace lawyers. Her account particularly reinforces buyer-side sourcing decisions and the growing role of alternative pricing, while her limited firsthand evidence on ALSPs prevents stronger claims about provider disruption.
qs: And so as a way to facilitate or supplement and augment the work that they’re doing.
So they’re being much more refined about where the work goes instead of, we don’t do it here, therefore let’s use an outside counsel.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: McDonnell directly supports the proposition that technology can reduce routine legal workload and create capacity for strategic work. She distinguishes indirect capacity creation through faster contract review from a direct strategic application in global-trade scenario planning, while presenting reported savings as customer examples rather than universal proof.
qs: And that mail includes drafting agreements and doing contract review and  providing advice and what we’re seeing, especially if we use sort of Thomson Reuters General Counsel’s office as an example, if they can reduce the time it takes to review a contract, that could free up time for them to do more strategic work.
So everybody’s talking about tariffs and how important and critical it is for global trade and using that product to do scenario planning.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: McDonnell supports the cluster’s core proposition that corporate legal departments selectively disaggregate work and choose providers task by task. She distinguishes complex work that may go to law firms from repetitive work suitable for ALSPs, while emphasizing cost control and accuracy rather than wholesale law-firm replacement. She does not materially address AI-driven pricing reform, junior training or verification risks.
qs: The other is they’re looking to see, where do I tactically outsource?

kp.k: True agents require planning, tools, and adaptive execution
kp.d: In the introductory segment, Nikki Shaver reports Dan Hoadley of vLex's definition: agents must use tools to act, reason about tool selection, plan toward goals, adapt during execution, and recognise completion. She reports that the conference panel found very few true agents in legal technology under this definition, distinguishing substantive capabilities from marketing terminology.
qs: Dan Hoadley of vLex produced a very clear definition. He says that essentially an agent has to have agency.

True agents are able to come up with a plan about how to accomplish the overall goal, then pursue that plan and make adjustments to the plan during execution, and they will know when the overall goal is accomplished.
The panel at our event actually concluded that based on Dan’s definition, there are very few true agents in the legal tech space at the moment.

kp.k: Agent procurement requires visibility and opportunities for intervention
kp.d: Shaver recommends different vendor questions for true agents than for assistant tools. Specifically, firms should investigate whether users can inspect an agent's proposed plan and correct it before execution in a legal workflow.
qs: the questions you should be asking your vendor if you’re dealing with a true agent are different than if you’re dealing with, for example, an assistant tool.

you may want to know whether visibility has been built in so that you can see the plan the agent creates for achieving its overall goal before it gets going on that plan and whether the lawyer or user is able to course correct the plan before it is executed.

kp.k: Automation could reposition corporate professionals as strategic partners
kp.d: McDonnell argues that automating repetitive work and accelerating research and workflows frees corporate legal, tax, and finance professionals for higher-order thinking and business strategy. She presents this as changing their perceived role from cost centres and risk gatekeepers to contributors to growth, risk reduction, and transformation; this is her account of the technology's value, rather than a measured finding about role changes.
qs: Sometimes folks might think about these groups as being cost centers.

the opportunity to do repetitive tasks that may be ones that don’t require a lot of higher order sort of thinking to free up time so you can do just that and become a strategic partner to the business.
We see that role, the role of the professional in the tax department or finance department or legal department, dramatically changing.

kp.k: Reported efficiencies include contract review and outside counsel spending
kp.d: McDonnell reports that Thomson Reuters' own general counsel's office reduced contract review time by 80 % plus using its products. She also cites an unnamed financial services company saving millions of dollars on outside counsel spend using Legal Tracker. These are vendor-reported examples without sample sizes, measurement periods, or methodological details; the transcript does not establish that AI alone produced the savings.
qs: So they’ve leveraged our products and they’ve been able to reduce contract review time by 80 % plus.

We’ve seen a financial services company looking at the work that they do and that is working with outside counsel and knowing that they’re getting a lot of pressure to reduce the cost, reduce the expenses, so using legal tracker to save millions of dollars on outside counsel spend.

kp.k: Trade scenario planning extends technology beyond immediate task completion
kp.d: Asked whether clients have broader transformation strategies, McDonnell identifies global trade management as a particularly direct example. She describes using captured data and extracted insights for tariff-related scenario planning and comparing future options, rather than merely resolving current issues.
qs: Probably the one that’s most direct, I think, is global trade management.

Not just sort of solving for the issue at hand, but being able to look around the corners, be able to predict what might happen in the future. Look at option A and option B and decide what we’re to go next.

kp.k: Legal sourcing increasingly weighs cost, quality, and task suitability
kp.d: McDonnell describes general counsel choosing among internal delivery, law firms, and ALSPs according to cost, accuracy, expertise, complexity, and task type, including repetitive work and e-discovery. Referring to a survey/report without providing its methodology or period, she says 'Like 35 %' of GCs are thinking about cost savings, while emphasising that correctness also matters.
qs: Like 35 % of GCs are thinking about cost savings, but they’re also wanting it to be done right.
It’s a repetitive task. Maybe that goes to the ALSP. Maybe it’s something around e-discovery.
So they’re being much more refined about where the work goes instead of, we don’t do it here, therefore let’s use an outside counsel.

kp.k: Provider technology and alternative billing enter buyer value assessments
kp.d: McDonnell says corporate buyers consider whether law firms and ALSPs use AI to augment their work and improve outcomes, and expects value-based billing and other arrangements to become important. She does not establish which provider category is more innovative: when Lambert asks that question, she explicitly limits her personal experience of ALSP conversations.
qs: So I wonder if the ALSP is leveraging AI, is the law firm leveraging AI? And so as a way to facilitate or supplement and augment the work that they’re doing.
different ways of billing, whether it’s value-based or other kinds of arrangements are going to be really important.
I haven’t personally encountered the conversations with ALSPs.

kp.k: Transformation requires stakeholder alignment and continuous learning
kp.d: McDonnell recommends aligning change with C-suite priorities, organisational purpose, and values, alongside repeated communication and resilient teams. Describing Thomson Reuters' own transformation, she says the corporate segment shifted from product-first selling to understanding customer needs before acting. She links legal critical thinking, business understanding, technology, and a growth mindset as complementary capabilities for navigating change.
qs: this is requiring them to have a really close relationship with their stakeholders, their C-suite, to really understand what are the key priorities that may be driving a change.
we shifted to become more customer-centric.
You’ve got law, you’ve got business, you’ve got technology. When you bring all of those together, for example, from a sales perspective, it’s about learning to put the customer at the center.
developing a team that’s resilient, that has the growth mindset.

kp.k: McDonnell frames AI as augmentation rather than workforce replacement
kp.d: McDonnell identifies analytics, pattern recognition, and routine process automation as the best current uses of generative and agentic AI. She rejects replacement as the intended role of these tools, instead arguing that AI proficiency affects individual employability. Her position is an augmentation claim, not empirical evidence that jobs will remain unaffected.
qs: What we’re seeing is that the best uses of generative AI or agentic AI are really about analytics.
It helps with automating routine processes. Once again, freeing up your time so you can be much more strategic.
The AI tool is only there to augment, not to replace.
if you don’t know AI, you’re going to be replaced by somebody who does.

kp.k: Human oversight and professional accountability remain essential
kp.d: McDonnell recommends ethical review boards, fairness and transparency checks, auditing, data governance, quality control, and training. She says humans must retain oversight and lawyers remain accountable for work produced with AI, comparing this responsibility to supervising paralegal work. She refers generically to the code of professional responsibility without identifying a jurisdiction or specific rule.
qs: You need to look at forming an ethical review board.
How do you audit to make sure that there’s no unintended consequences from that work?
The human needs to provide oversight.
according to the code of professional responsibility, whether you have a paralegal or you have an AI, you’re still responsible. You’re still accountable for the work product.

kp.k: Predictive reasoning is a conditional future capability
kp.d: In response to a question about the next five to ten years, McDonnell anticipates AI developing toward predictive analytics, risk assessment, and legal reasoning that approaches aspects of human judgment. She gives no specific delivery date and explicitly raises reliability testing, domain expertise, human checking, and continued oversight as conditions for value.
qs: But what about the future? Can we use it to predict? Is it reliable? How do we test to make sure it’s reliable?
Risk assessment, legal reasoning. And so these topics start adding in a layer of judgment.
But I could see where over time, genitive AI and agentic AI has a level of skill that could sort of border on that judgment assessment, what we normally would expect from a human.
powered by domain expertise and humans checking, it could be of value.

kp.k: Future AI may integrate advice across corporate functions
kp.d: McDonnell envisages insights spanning legal, tax, trade, and compliance rather than isolated departmental answers. Her hypothetical manufacturing plant in Malaysia illustrates interconnected employment law, employment policy, manager training, supplier, and third-party questions. This is a proposed future use, not a documented implementation.
qs: it’s not just legal or just tax or just compliance, but you have the opportunity to draw insights across legal tax trade compliance.
You want to establish a manufacturing plant in Malaysia, you’re to have a series of questions that are not just legal.
And I can see the insights being drawn no matter what the source is, no matter what the content that.

kp.k: Skills shortages motivate employer-supported AI training
kp.d: McDonnell reports customer concerns about shortages of qualified lawyers and CPAs who are prepared to use technology. She predicts increasing demand for skilled professionals and recommends company-supported AI training, continuous learning, and resilient teams, rather than presenting a quantified labour-market forecast.
qs: They’re talking about the shortages that are out there in terms of folks who are qualified to, whether they’re a CPA or a lawyer.
There’s going to be an even more increased demand for skilled professionals. It’ll continue.
We’re looking for our companies to help us with that because technology is going to be able to be used for us to get ahead.
How do you develop this high performance team that is willing to embrace the changes that occur and be able to continue to deliver and continue to learn?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McDonnell says AI automation and faster research can turn corporate legal, tax and finance professionals from perceived cost centres into strategic business partners.
pts.d: At 18:36–24:59, Laura Clayton McDonnell describes repetitive-task automation and faster access to answers as freeing time for higher-order thinking, strategic planning and business advice. She presents this as a transformation already underway through Thomson Reuters technology. Her concrete examples include an internally reported reduction of more than 80% in contract-review time and an unnamed financial-services company's savings on outside counsel through Legal Tracker. Those examples concern product use; the transcript does not isolate the contribution of AI to either result.

pts.k: McDonnell says corporate buyers increasingly consider providers' AI use when allocating work and assessing value.
pts.d: At 25:49–28:59, she describes GCs choosing among internal delivery, law firms and ALSPs according to cost, accuracy, specialisation, complexity and outcomes. AI is presented as a means of supplementing provider work, alongside growing importance for value-based and other billing arrangements. She treats ALSPs as continuing options rather than predicting that they will displace law firms. She does not endorse the host's suggestion of market bifurcation or identify which provider category is more innovative.

pts.k: McDonnell frames generative and agentic AI as augmentation rather than replacement, while predicting a competitive disadvantage for professionals who lack AI skills.
pts.d: At 33:34–36:33, she identifies analysis of large data volumes, pattern recognition and routine-process automation as the best current uses. She says these tools free humans for strategic thinking and decision-making, rather than eliminating their role. Separately, she warns that AI-skilled people will replace those without AI knowledge. At 37:02–40:11, she predicts increasing demand for skilled professionals, against a claimed existing shortage.

pts.k: McDonnell predicts AI will move toward predictive analytics, risk assessment and legal reasoning that approach human judgment, and toward insights spanning multiple corporate functions.
pts.d: At 37:02–40:11, she distinguishes current data analysis and routine work from prospective predictive and judgment-like capabilities. She also anticipates integrated insights across legal, tax, trade and compliance, illustrated by a hypothetical manufacturing plant in Malaysia requiring employment, hiring, supplier and third-party advice. These are prospective possibilities, not reported demonstrations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main support consists of McDonnell's customer experience, internal and unnamed customer examples, and a briefly cited survey; future capabilities are forecasts without benchmarks.
pts.d: McDonnell cites Thomson Reuters' own general counsel office for the more-than-80% contract-review reduction and an unnamed financial-services customer for millions of dollars saved through Legal Tracker. No baseline, sample, measurement period, quality comparison or AI-specific attribution is supplied. She cites a survey/report figure of about 35% of GCs thinking about cost savings, without identifying its methodology; this supports the cost-pressure context rather than proving AI outcomes. She explicitly acknowledges limited direct experience concerning ALSP conversations. Her augmentation, skilled-demand and future judgment claims rest on executive observations and expectations, not quantified labour-market evidence or performance tests. Her statement that lawyers remain accountable invokes professional responsibility generally, without naming a jurisdiction or rule.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current automation and buyer behaviour are distinguished from loosely timed future capabilities; human oversight, reliability testing and organisational preparation qualify the outlook.
pts.d: In this source labelled 2025, McDonnell presents automation, internal review-time savings and selective sourcing as current developments. Although the host asks about five to ten years, McDonnell does not explicitly commit her forecasts to that interval: she calls the future almost here but uses 'over time' for judgment-like capability. She questions predictive reliability and stresses domain expertise and human checking before reliance. Her augmentation model requires oversight, ethical review, accountability, auditing, data governance, quality control and training. Preparing for increased demand requires employer-supported AI learning and resilient teams willing to keep learning.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal and related functions, their business stakeholders, competing legal-service providers, and professionals needing AI skills.
pts.d: GCs and in-house teams are the buyers expected to manage constrained budgets, reduce routine work and outside counsel expenditure, and provide more strategic advice. Tax, finance, trade and compliance professionals are included in the same transformation and prospective cross-functional insights. Corporate executives and business stakeholders receive faster, broader advice on risk, growth and operations. Law firms and ALSPs face more selective sourcing and scrutiny of their cost, accuracy, outcomes and technology use. Lawyers and other skilled professionals must learn AI and retain responsibility for work product. McDonnell does not specify staffing reductions, entry-level displacement, firm staffing shapes or effects on unmet civil legal need.
